conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having really high blood sugars—like in the 400s. My PCP saw me yesterday for my leg ulcer and sent me here. I’ve been managing without insulin, but it’s not working anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned chest tightness and restlessness when your sugars are high. Are you having any chest pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not right now. But I’ve had that before when my sugar spikes. It goes away after I get insulin. I just don’t have a plan or meds at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We checked your blood sugar in the ER—it was 277, came down with fluids. Your EKG and chest X-ray look stable, no signs of a heart attack. We’ll keep an eye on your heart, but it seems your main issue is blood sugar control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So, I need insulin again? I was diet-controlled for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. With your recent leg procedure and wound, your body is under stress, which can worsen diabetes. Plus, your diabetes may be progressing. We’re starting you on a mix of insulin—75-25, 5 units twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: 5 units? That’s not too much, right? I’m sensitive to insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly why we’re starting low. We’ll monitor you closely. You’ll also use a sliding scale if your sugars go high. The goal is to avoid lows while getting better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds safe. What about my leg? The ulcer’s still open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular surgery saw you. No signs of infection. They recommend wet-to-dry dressings. It’s healing slowly, which is expected with your circulation issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t feel the pulses in my feet. Is that normal for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, due to your peripheral vascular disease, circulation is poor. That’s why wounds heal slowly. Keep the dressing clean and follow up with your vascular doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my heart? I’ve had chest pain before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG shows old changes, no new damage. Your chest pain sounds like stable angina. We’ll keep you on your usual meds—Plavix, beta-blocker, aspirin, and others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take nitroglycerin if it flares up. It helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Use it as needed. We’ll also continue your dialysis tomorrow. Your kidney function is stable, so we’ll aim to get you to dry weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on dialysis for years. That part’s routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure it goes smoothly. Now, about the insulin—we’ll teach you how to give it. You’ll check your sugar in the morning, before meals, and at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Six times a day? That’s a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s important at first to see how your body responds. Once it’s stable, you might reduce frequency. We’ll help you adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your fasting sugar was 142 this morning—much better. You’re responding well to the insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I gave my first shot last night. Was a little nervous, but it went okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great job. We’ll keep monitoring. No signs of low sugar so far. Your dialysis is scheduled for this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to go home after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well—yes. You’re stable, no chest pain, sugars improving. We just need to confirm you’re safe on the new insulin plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. You’re at your dry weight, and your breathing is easy. No fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel lighter. And I haven’t had any swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your chest X-ray still shows a stable small fluid collection, but no pulmonary edema. Your heart is handling things well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my heel pain? I have an appointment for that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have an appointment with ortho for bilateral heel pain. It’s likely related to your walking pattern and circulation. Keep using supportive shoes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars stayed in the 100s all day. No lows. That’s excellent. We think you’re ready for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can you go over the insulin again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’ll take 5 units of 75-25 insulin under the skin with breakfast and dinner. Always check your sugar before giving it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it’s low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s below 60, drink juice or eat a snack. Always carry something with sugar. And call your doctor if it keeps happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And my other meds stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly yes. We’re switching your stomach medicine from Nexium to pantoprazole. Same dose, once a day. And your metoprolol is now 50 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can manage that. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see a new diabetologist and a nutritionist. Also, vascular and ortho for your leg and heel. Keep weighing yourself daily—call if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home. You’ve done well on insulin, no issues. Here’s your discharge packet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing I have a plan now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: check sugars 6–8 times a day, take insulin as prescribed, and keep your appointments. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if my leg looks worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call vascular or come in. Signs like redness, swelling, or pus mean you need to be seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again for your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up, and I’m confident you’ll do well with this new routine.
